utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case Number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, today we are hearing a new witness. Can she please stand up and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Defence, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mrs. Radovanovic. Can you hear me well, and can you hear the -- could you hear the interpretation when Her Honour the Presiding Judge addressed you? Before you begin your today's testimony, I'd like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the following: To begin with, the first thing has to do with Mrs. Radovanovic's stay here. She told me that on Wednesday she has a class in Banja Luka. Because this is the end of the year, and the university courses are coming to the end, she needs to be there. She need not finish today, but if she could finish earlier tomorrow. I've already discussed it with Mr. Di Fazio, and I've told Mr. Di Fazio, and I've already told Your Honours that I will need about an hour for my examination in chief, and Mr. Di Fazio said that his examination might last one hour -- an hour and a half or two. So I believe that we could finish also the redirect today. I merely wished to tell this, Your Honour, so that you have some idea as to how long the examination of this witness would last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the information. I just hope that both parties will try as much as possible to deal with the most relevant parts to the evidence of the witness. We have had the report for some days now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. The second thing I wish to mention has to do with two mathematical errors in the work. These are only two figures which were erroneously typed, and if need be, we should type it additionally during the break, and then introduce it as a correction in an annex. In the English version on page 16, and on page 21 in B/C/S version, there is a table, number 4. And in table number 4 under Croats, and percentages, I am talking about the fourth column, third line, instead of 290, it has to be 29. You will see how it all adds up to 100, so this 0 here is a typo, because in B/C/S, they put decimals, and that is why the mistake. The second error which occurred, which Ms. Radovanovic noticed when she went through the original, is the correction, English text page 14, and B/C/S 19. In the line 4 in the English version, from the bottom, figure 1.402, 1.402 Muslims. Instead of that figure, it should be 1.812. This is an error which Ms. Radovanovic spotted and asked me to inform you. If need be, we shall submit these corrections in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say something. It is not -- in the first table that you mentioned; it is 29.0. It is not 29, but 29.0. Not 290, but 29.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we will explain it all to the Chamber. I believe it is all quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Radovanovic, we shall begin discussing your work. I will now ask you, I've already drawn your attention, since the two of us speak the same language, will you please wait until my question is fully ended and then start answering so that the interpreters can have time to interpret what we are saying. And the interpreters have also been supplied with copies of your text. Will you introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Svetlana Radovanovic, and shall I also tell you something about my CV or what am I supposed to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only your name. In front of you, you have your paper. Will you tell us if your signature figures on the last page of this work.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the number, please. Can we have the number for this expert analysis which we are tendering. Of course, it has to do with all three Defences, but it can be Mr. Tadic's Defence or whichever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will be admitted as Exhibit D196/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, just on that issue that -- I'm sorry. As far as the number to be assigned to it, Mr. Lukic just said that the report is part of the Defence of all three defendants. Is it their position that they accept -- that all three defendants accept the conclusions and the substance of the report? Because I understood that it was only part of the Defence of Mr. Tadic. I'm not quarrelling with, that but we want to be absolutely crystal clear about this. All three defendants adopt the position in the report? I see counsel nodding, so I assume that I'm correct in that. Thank you very much, and I apologise for my interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm on behalf of Mr. Zaric's Defence that we also stand by this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the same position is also for Dr. Simic Defence. And I would like just to respectfully remind my learned friend that we filed our joint motion at the beginning of the Defence case, designated our joint experts, including Dr. Radovanovic. So everything is in file. Maybe it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've very grateful to Mr. Pantelic for pointing that out to me. So we're now absolutely clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just wondering about the curriculum vitae. I thought it could have a slash or something, from the registry assistant, just to separate it from the report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The biography in English will be treated as Exhibit D196/3, D196A/3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, I will first ask you a few brief questions concerning your curriculum vitae since the curriculum vitae that we have attended, we hear about the experience, professional experience. And so I will have to -- but it is very short. So will you please tell the Court where do you work now? Except that I think that your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I work at the faculty of geography of the University of Belgrade. I'm head of department for demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that department, there are, I presume, several subjects. What do you teach?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I teach introduction to demography [realtime transcript read in error "democracy"], basic statistics of the population, and ethnodemography.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I believe is important -- will you please repeat, but slowly, the first two subjects that you teach.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Introduction to demography [realtime transcript read in error "democracy"], to its introduction to the science, and then basics of fundamentals of statistics and population statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but we have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, on the same note, Mr. Lukic, are we talking about democracy, which is what is written here, or demography?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I teach demography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We see "democracy" written twice here. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I think is important in your analysis, and for our case, is what it says in your CV, that you work for the state statistics administration, or as it says here, Institute of Serbia. What we'd like to know in particular, in view of the source of information, what we'd like to know is where did you work in 1991 and tell us in a few words how long did you work at that institution?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the state statistics administration of Serbia I worked from 1974 to 1991, until December 1991. From 1986 to December 1991, I headed the population statistics department. I participated directly as a methodologist, as a member of expert teams, inter-republican, I mean, in the former Yugoslavia, in population censuses in 1981 and 1991, and indirectly in the census population of 1971. I conducted the population census in Serbia in 1991 as I was the head of the department. So this was as official, and I was the secretary of the Population Census Bureau of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell the Court what novelties, if there were any novelties that were introduced in the population census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The novelty was in the first place the manner of data processing, since on the eve of the census, or rather a few months before that, it was decided at the federal level to apply completely different forms from those which were used in the previous census. The decision to use these new forms was explained that it would speed up the census because, in view of the technological innovations, it would be possible to scan the material and computerise the whole processing. I was against it throughout the process, however, this decision was taken at the level of the SFRY, only Macedonia refused it and refused to conduct the census whereas all the other republics used these new computerised forms to conduct the censuses in their territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And my last question relative to your general experience with the population censuses will be: What did the results show at the federal level and what drew your attention regarding this new form of forms and electronic reading?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My personal experience and experience in all other republics, especially Croatia which had already done it in 1991, is that it made the feeding in of data slow down, because scanning constituted a major problem. When we're scanning and feeding in the data, terrible substitutions took place so that we had to slow down the feeding of data into computers as we had to intervene all the time. And I would like to show you something to simply explain what that means, I mean how it made matters complicated. The new forms, the new forms which we received a few months -- when I say "we," I mean the territory of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please slow down. Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Necessitated a certain, not to say a special manner of taking down information, and it had to do both with figures and things which are in letters. If you take the methodology of the census population of 1991, and I'd like really to see it -- I do not know if you can see it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is, it was exactly explained what the shape of every character should be and every numeral, what they should look like, because we were told if they didn't look as they should, then it could become complicated. And that complication really occurred later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We shall come back to it if need be. And if necessary, we shall copy it and submit it to the Trial Chamber. Now, I'd like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. I'm just wondering, when the witness mentions on page 7, line 20, you see it says: "The new forms, the new forms which we received a few months," a few months when? It's really quite unclear as it stands in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain. You said a few months before, but what did you mean by that? A few months before what?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The population census is performed on the date of midnight of the 31st of March. So a few months before the census takes place, we start getting ready, preparing the methodology, the forms, and so on and so forth. And before that, a pilot census made in order to check whether the forms are all right and whether the questions are formulated properly. So we did this trial census perhaps two years or perhaps three on the forms that were ready for the census of 1991. However, towards the end of 1990, and I cannot say exactly whether it was October or November, it was decided that new forms should be used for this census. That is, the format would be completely new. It wasn't the contents which changed, but the format was completely different, and necessitated something that earlier censuses did not necessitate, that is, the recorders had to either introduce only letters, which is characteristic, for instance, of Bosnia, or numerals and characters, except that these forms did not include the explanations as was the case in earlier censuses. So that this didn't come as a surprise only for us who were working there, because we had to translate our whole methodology to suit a new format, but I also think that it was a shortcoming for those who were conducting the censuses because it necessitated a completely different approach and attention was drawn to us that one had to use very special ballpoints, that figures and letters had to be written in a particular way. Now, if you have in mind that we had about 100.000 people who were involved, who were either instructors or pollsters, it is obviously that it was too short a time to train all these people to write as precisely as required. And then there were so many substitutions. I can go into that, but that was hair-raising. That is, when you read the material, if the figure is not written as was required, then number 1 can be read like 7 or like 4 or like 1, and so on and so forth. And of course for statistics, this is very important, because every figure in statistics is a code which tells a great deal. So for instance, if you say marital status or single is 1, divorcee means 3, separated 4, and so on and so forth, and it's very important to have these exact numerals there. And that is why very complicated situations happened when you received results which produce a completely distorted picture. In my paper, I wrote it down in relation to the ethnic structure that for instance, in a locality -- for instance, in a locality in Serbia, the figures which we got was that it was the English man with Danish as the mother tongue, or the other way around; Danes with the English mother tongue. So of course one had to intervene in all this material because you know only too well that such people do not live there. But such errors were merely the result of the substitution rather than the ignorance of pollsters or somebody else. And I could quote you a whole string of examples like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we've already clarified it. Mrs. Radovanovic, we'll have to cut your answers short, nevertheless make it quite clear to the Trial Chamber, because that is why you are here, but please cut your answers shorter. Now a few questions so that we can clarify what was the methodology used in your analysis that you drew for the Defence. Did you read the analysis submitted by the expert for the Prosecution, by Mrs. Ewa Tabeau and Jakob Brijeg [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement of her -- the record of her testimony before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you just tell us very briefly, what was the task that the Defence put before you when we asked you to do this analysis?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Defence asked me if I could do a correct and proper analysis of the demographic structure in the two municipalities, and to see whether for such a study, there were sources which could be accepted as reliable and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And will you tell the Court, because this is something that we insisted on, why did you think it was important to go into the scanned information that the Prosecution had, or rather, the census lists and the census applications?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I read the expert opinion of the experts for the Prosecution, I had numerous doubts regarding the quality of data, and especially the identification numbers and the names. However, I wished to check whether I was right to suspect that this information was not correct. So I went through that material, and I'm afraid that I was right to doubt, and it concerns especially the identification and numbers. I must say that the identification numbers were for the first time collected at the level of Yugoslavia in 1991. They were never controlled, and none of the former republics never used them for any purpose. When I say "purpose," I mean official purpose. Of course, I can explain why this was collected, if somebody wants to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll address that issue later. We'll now move on to certain matters that need to be clarified in your report. I'd like to point out that with regard to the report, that the Trial Chamber is familiar with, we will not discuss the contents of the report, but we'll just try to clarify some matters that weren't quite clear to me. And I assume that these issues might be of interest to the Trial Chamber. It might be useful to clarify these issues. First of all, I will put a few questions to you, few questions that you dealt with and that have to do with the analysis of the declaration of one's nationality. I think that was something quite new for me. I'll draw the Trial Chamber's attention to paragraph 13 and to paragraph 14 and 15. There's a table there, too. In paragraph 13, I'll now read through it very slowly, it's the second sentence. "Thus only general and rough statistics could be obtained --"

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, paragraph 13 is not the same in my version. Is that the B/C/S version? The origin of sources of information?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, I'm reading the second sentence. I apologise. "Thus only general and rough statistics could be obtained on certain features, such as ethnic affiliation, because the answer -- and this is what's important to me -- because the answer to this question was often influenced by ideology." I would also like to draw your attention to the middle of paragraph 15 when you carried out that analysis and came to the conclusion that in both municipalities it served, the indicator of the dynamics of change of the number of Serbs and Croats showed significant oscillations, and what is important to me is that they cannot be counted for by realistic demographic explanations. And so the only logical conclusion is that there was a change of attitude from census to census when declaring ethnic affiliation. What I'm interested in in relation to your report, which is quite clear, is whether this was characteristic only for the municipality of Samac and Odzak, or was this something that was also characteristic for a wider area in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's characteristic for the wider area of Yugoslavia, for all those who are involved in statistics or in demographics. It was something that was characteristic for the entire Yugoslav area, and if you follow the censuses in various areas, you can obtain information that could be contested. And why could such information be contested? Because there are such oscillations, such fluctuations that can't be demographically explained because you need time for demographic processes. Nothing happens overnight, naturally, apart from certain tectonic disturbances, et cetera. So if a census is taken every ten years, you have five or six censuses, 48, 61, if you have six censuses, and you have such great fluctuations with regard to certain nationalities, then this can't be explained demographically. However, there is a explanation. According to this explanation, the criteria used - and this is something that is part of the methodology - the criterion that is used when trying to obtain an answer to what one's nationality is, the criterion is a subjective one. It is a criterion which means that at a given point in time, you can declare yourself to be whatever you want to be. The census taker had to record what individuals declared, so if in times of tension, then the interviewee would have to give various answers for various reasons, perhaps fear, perhaps subjective feelings. And this subjective feeling with regard to declaring one's nationality is the cause of such significant fluctuations. This is very characteristic in many communities, for example Yugoslavs, and then certain small ethnic groups, the Roma, so these situations change depending on the census, depending on the situation, and that is why it can't be explained demographically. What can explain this is the fact that people made various declarations for various censuses. There are quite a number of works that deal with this matter. You also have to take into consideration the period -- the historical period concerned, the social organisation within which we lived, and in that system, they tried to deal with the national question as one that had been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the technical booth, if possible, to lower the ELMO as I don't have a direct view of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we will address an issue that is very significant to me. This concerns people, guest workers abroad, and you spoke about this in paragraph 16 and 17, and in table number 2. First of all, a simple question that I will put to you: Citizens who were temporarily working abroad, were they treated as a special category during the census of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. In none of the censuses from 1971, which is when we started obtaining information for them, right up to 1991, this category of citizens were treated as the permanent inhabitants of their places of residence regardless of -- regardless of their location at the time of the census and regardless of the period of time spent there. So they could have spent 20 years away from their place from which they were originally, but they were Yugoslavs and that was taken to be their permanent home, and they were recorded as permanent citizens of the -- of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, 1.420 people were born abroad in that census. What does that indicate, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that shows that it was perhaps the third generation living abroad. People started leaving in the mid-1960s, and this third generation, perhaps they never even saw their place of origin. Perhaps they had never even been in Yugoslavia, but they were recorded as permanent citizens of, in this case, Samac, and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when an analysis is carried out, such as the one that you carried out with the purpose of determining the migration of the population in these two municipalities during a specific period of time - we're interested in 1992 and 1993 - in such cases, must these citizens be included in the mass of population or excluded from it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be more logical to exclude them from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: However it's not just a matter of migration, it's a matter that concerns the ethnic composition of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm making a mistake. I would now like to have a look at paragraph 20. We would like to talk about personal identification numbers, but this matter that you explained a minute ago, you said that these identification numbers were first used in the census of 1991. And the last sentence that I'm going to read also concerns our observation of the census material. This was evident during our examination of the census material which revealed an extremely large number of inaccurately recorded first and last names and nonexistent, inaccurate, or duplicated personal identification numbers. More than 40 per cent in Odzak, and more than 31 percent in Samac you said on direct examination. On what basis did you come to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the date now, I can't remember when we were there. That was last month. But I'll have to have a look. From the 14th to the 16th of April, 2003, we were granted permission to directly examine the documents. And by doing this, we came to the conclusion, or rather, we confirmed what we had suspected; namely, that it was a matter of statistical characteristics that contained so many errors that it was quite useless in statistical terms. You couldn't make any claims on the basis of such information. You couldn't claim that you had a reliable source of such information. And on that occasion, we came to the conclusion that about 40 per cent of the population in Odzak, and over 31 per cent of the population in Samac had erroneous or incorrect personal identification numbers, or nonexistent personal identification numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have such defective census information, can this be relevant to indicate -- as to be used in statistical demographic research?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not just a matter of the defects. There are many other problems that are involved. In addition to those defects, there are a lot of failings. I said that 40 per cent is not correct; that doesn't mean that the 60 per cent that is correct was used in an appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to the electoral lists from 1971, I will go back to paragraph 11 where you say -- and I need this to be clarified so I believe that the Trial Chamber will need this clarification too. In the last sentence, you say that such a sample is not representative and has been reduced twice, first in terms of ethnic identity, and secondly, it was reduced to the administrative and territorial borders from 1997. Could you perhaps clarify what you wanted to say when addressing the matter of electoral lists.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, it was replicated on three occasions, not just twice, and first of all it related to the personal identification numbers. The second time, it concerned the ethnical composition, and the third time it concerned the territorial sense. What does it mean to say the personal identification numbers? You mean you have 40 per cent of the population whose personal identification numbers are nonexistent, but since they do not exist you exclude this segment of the population and you don't take them into consideration when you compare them with the electoral list. So you yourself perform a reduction. Among those 40 per cent, there must have been some who were on the electoral list, but they can't be coupled up because there are no -- there's no information that would allow you to do this, or it's very difficult to do this. That is the first reduction. The second one, which concerns ethnic affiliation, the lists don't have information on ethnic affiliation. Ethnic affiliation with regard to the electoral list is taken, is adopted from the census of 1991. In 1997 and 1998, if you can find me, you'll link me -- you'll take my information on ethnic membership and you will make it correspond to the relevant year. If the personal identification numbers were correct, if you were able to couple this up successfully, namely, with regard to Svetlana Radovanovic, and then you use my statement that I made eight years ago, very well. But what if you do it on the basis of the name, the first and last name and the initials? In such a case, are you really taking over what was declared to be one's ethnic affiliation in 1991? So this is the second reduction that occurs. The reduction on the territorial basis is as follows: You have a framework which was valid in 1991, and you have a framework instituted by the Dayton agreement in 1995. This framework, from 1995, and the framework from 1991 do not overlap in territorial terms because places are divided. The Dayton agreement caused division among certain villages, certain places. When you have such places that were divided, it's not possible to statistically calculate who from the population went to the left side and who to the right side. So what do you do? What do the experts do? What are the Prosecution's experts doing? They are excluding those places, those villages, and pretending that they don't exist, or rather, the population from those places. If they followed this principle through to the end, there would be no problem. If they exclude this in 1991, but in 1997 or 1998 they make partial use of it or they don't use it at all, and this is very easy to prove, and this is the mistake that they have made. I doubt that it was intentional but they made this mistake because in statistical terms they can't cover the tame territory, because in 1991, in addition to the code for the municipality, you have a code for a village, for a place. And a municipality is composed of several places, several villages. In 1997, you only have new codes for municipalities, you don't have any for villages. So you don't know, even if you were willing to know about this, if you don't know about the villages from 1991, you don't know where to place the population that you found somewhere because there are certain villages, certain places that are missing. And then you make errors. You're comparing two different territorial entities but you claim to be comparing the same territorial entity. And this is methodologically not allowable. It's very evident, it's very obvious because there are surpluses that appear, and this hasn't been explained in the case of the Prosecution. But I can claim that this is the result of the fact that there is a lack -- the territory of municipalities don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we have a look at paragraph 29 in your work now, because I think that that is where the subject that you are discussing now is addressed. I'm going to read the second sentence. This is what interests me. "Leaving aside the question as to whether this sample is good or not, you mentioned the sample that you coupled up earlier on, which is quite similar to what the Prosecution mentioned, we shall point to the fact this is not the sample that the said experts used as the basis for their conclusions on changes in the ethnic structure."

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite clear when you look at the information from the Prosecution's expert. Their experts in certain tables provided one figure of those who had been coupled, and when they distribute this on the basis of the newly formed municipalities, the number, the figures is quite different. And I can show that the result is absurd. For example, in the table for Bosanski Samac, the Prosecution's experts say -- I've got the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute so that this is clear for the transcript. The witness is now looking at the Prosecution's report, P133 of the B/C/S version. That's for the sake of the numbers of the tables. Perhaps you could put it on the ELMO, and then explain those numbers.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to look at those numbers, but I'll put something else on the ELMO. I apologise. This is Odzak. I want to put Bosanski Samac on the ELMO. For example, table 3 shows everything that the Prosecution experts matched up and, as they said, identified, so it means that someone who was Svetlana Radovanovic in 1991, this person they found in 1997 and 1998 by using the personal identification number and the name. So such identified individuals, they found 14.315 of them, but they were not able to locate them later on. Before I move on to the tables, I would just like to mention the number of Serbs. In Bosanski Samac, the Prosecution experts claim that they identified 7.704 Serbs. And when they carry out a division, they have 10.000 -- could you please have a look at table -- just a minute. 5B, table 6A in the Prosecution expert report. If you compare table 3 where they say that they identified 7.704 Serbs with table 6A where they claim that they have 10.362 Serbs on the electoral list, then it's quite incredible to see that you have 7.000, but you're also talking about the figure of over 10.000. So they have claimed that there are over 35 per cent of Serbian individuals on the electoral list. And this is interesting. This is also applicable to Odzak. It's interesting to have a look at tables 7 and 8 which show the number of electors who haven't been assigned to any category. I'll now mention table 8, page 27 in the Serbian version, after paragraph 49. A total 14.315 were identified, according to the Prosecution's expert, when they were distributed on the basis of the newly formed municipalities, and then you have 2.486 electors, and they weren't able to distribute them. They didn't know what to do with them because the methodology that was used was not correct because they neglected the territorial level, and they compared apples and pears.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's just something else that I would like to say. Here you can quite clearly see that you have a number of electors who have been identified, a number that has not been identified, located, and it's not a clear number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just make it for clear that you meant your table 7.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It isn't. In my analysis, this is not my table. This is the table of the Prosecution expert. In my case, it is table 8, table 8. And -- but there is, however, the source. Ewa Tabeau, these are the tables which are 6A, 5B, and 6B which were taken over from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move to another topic, but we won't be talking much about that topic. I'd rather like you to explain in a few words, because it is frequently mentioned in your analysis and in Prosecution's, what is the personal identification number of a citizen? What is that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to explain, it means their first, last name, the year of birth, the principle characteristics of every individual. In the former Yugoslavia, its introduction started in 1982. And it includes -- it has 13 figures. These 13 figures, the first seven are the day, month and year of birth, then there are two numerals which indicate the area where you are registered, where you were assigned this, three figures indicating your gender, and the third one is derived. In the former Yugoslavia, there is a law on the identification number, so one knows exactly who and how assigns identification numbers, and there is a specific instruction, an official one, as to how identification numbers are controlled. Because they cannot be repeated, or rather, it simply should not happen in the former Yugoslavia to this day, because I do not think that anyone has done anything in this regard in the former republics. It should not happen to have two individuals with the same identification number in a territory. Now, if you allow me, because I haven't finished, these identification numbers, as I have said, they are made of 13 figures which can be good or bad, that is, they can be good insofar as the structure is concerned and bad because they are inaccurate. You can write down 13 figures, but when you start checking it, you see that these figures were just invented, that is they simply do not tally. They can be complete and accurate. That is, you have these 13 figures, and it is precise because it is accurate and it does mean Svetlana Radovanovic. Or it can be incomplete, which automatically means that they are not good when one is controlling an identification number because they simply contain the information about the same date of birth. These identification numbers were introduced, and I think a number of advanced countries have such numbers. In 1991, they were for the first time included in the population census.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: With the view to make population registers based on population censuses and these numbers, such as developed countries have. However, this idea was thwarted for the simple reason that it was noted, and I am speaking about Serbia, but I think it holds true of the rest of the Yugoslav territory with the exception of Slovenia, because it was noted that the information was not good. Nobody can change one's identification number. I mean, there is a whole procedure if one embarks on this. And secondly, I was against the incorporation of identification numbers, and never in the census, either in 1991 or in 2002 in the census in Serbia, I did not give the pollsters the information about the identification number because I think this is a violation of privacy, and I think that a large number of people think that because that has nothing to do with statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to move on somewhat faster because there are a few more topics we have to cover. Paragraph 35, and I believe that the Chamber is quite clear about duplication of identification numbers, about incomplete numbers, and so on and so forth. But what I found curious was relevant information in paragraph 35, when you speak about names, about first and last names.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 35A, the last sentence -- excuse me, sorry, 35C, the last sentence, that you established that in Odzak, 589 individuals in Odzak had identical names, father's names, and last names, and that about 10 per cent of them even had identical identification numbers, and then you give your comment.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we established, and that automatically means that the source of information is highly suspicious. Generally speaking, to use such a source, of course, brings into question all the findings. I'd like to underline, if you have duplicated identification numbers in such numbers, and so many duplicated names and last names, then there is always a risk, then you find one person, but you've found ten such persons. Ten duplicated identification numbers mean the following: If we have an identification number in 1991, say, of Svetlana Radovanovic, if it repeats ten times --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you match them, then you have -- and you see it only once in the list, but you put on the identification number, and then you match it ten times with the identification number of Svetlana Radovanovic in the list with one identification number, and you are showing that you've matched, that is, identified, ten individuals. Sorry, that is absolutely inaccurate because you've identified only one individual, but because of all these doubles, the procedure is such that you have to say, "I matched so-and-so many" because they were matched indeed except that this duplicate shows that the quality of identification numbers in population censuses is highly doubtful because the pollsters were instructed to attach special attention when taking down identification numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to paragraph 37, because to my mind, this is one of the crucial paragraphs in your whole expertise. And I'll read out to you a sentence which is somewhere in the middle of this paragraph, and we are talking about the distribution of persons without the municipality code number.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said what number?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Number 37. The sentence is: "It seems it would appear the person from this category without a code are treated according to the displaced persons living abroad. This is unacceptable. If it is not indicated how many members of this group are migrants." I do not know, why doesn't it say that they are migrants.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is no single information in our OSCE list which says we are making a census of migrant workers. They even talk about Bosnia and Herzegovinian citizens, but citizens, that is. You do not have a single information from the OSCE list that shows that they are displaced persons. And in view of the number of migrants abroad, migrant workers abroad --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, do go on.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- the number of these persons who are treated as displaced persons by the Prosecution's expert are very likely those citizens, that is, those migrant workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at what should be the result of your method of the manner in which you used these results. These are tables 4 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Just one little question before you move on, Mr. Lukic. From your sort of expert point of view, how would you differentiate between a displaced person working abroad and a migrant worker working abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I quite understand you. If you are talking about people who were abroad in 1991 already, then I do not see how such a person can be treated as a displaced person. He is registered as a citizen of Samac or Odzak, and perhaps has a house or some farm or perhaps nothing, perhaps lived in the parental home, and that person left in 1991, and perhaps he came every fifth year, perhaps every 15 years. Perhaps he never came back in 20 years' time, so that person is not a displaced person. Sure, there could have been people who are displaced because their house had been burned down, and that is how they feel like. But if you're asking me how one can tell apart people who are displaced abroad and those who are migrant workers abroad, I'm not sure I can do that, but I could if there is some kind of a reference point allowing us to establish whether they are migrant workers because, you know, very many of those workers have households where you still have grandparents, that is, somebody who can provide information about them, or there's nobody who can provide information about them. So at this moment, I cannot really tell them apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But whatever the case, in 1991, it was established who were those people who were migrant workers at that time abroad.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us look at your tables 4 and 6, and they show how you made the distributions according to your methodology. And two words only, and you can explain how you addressed the territorial principle. But would you say that this method is more reliable than any other when you have this kind of sources of information that were available both to you and to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, there is no reliable way to arrive at a reliable analysis. But in any event, it is statistically more accurate because you are dealing with a mass of people who you know where they are. We are not making assessments, we are not trying to make conjectures; do they belong to this or that category, whether they are displaced or not? That is, of those who are identified, those who had identification codes, we knew where to distribute them; and those who didn't, well, here they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we shall address a topic which you mention in your paragraphs 44, 45, 46, when you speak about the different localities in the municipalities of Samac and Odzak, and I would like to benefit from the presence of Mrs. Radovanovic here to analyse briefly something that frequently came up before this Court because His Honour Judge Lindholm asked Tadic about some settlements in the municipality of Samac. So I would like the expert witness to be shown a document. The witness will tell us what it is. The Defence has already supplied it to the Chamber, but we have a sufficient number of copies in both B/C/S and English. And here, will you please give Their Honours this. We shall not need them for a long time, but the Prosecution already has this. Your Honours, we frequently spoke about the territory which was, in fact, under the control of Serb authorities and part of the territory, the municipality which wasn't, and this is the part of the Defence thesis, especially when we refer to the indictment and figures mentioned in the indictment. Now, Mrs. Radovanovic, will you please, but please, let us wait a moment...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, might I just have a look at the document that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is simply blown up. I did provide it to the Prosecution on Friday. It was simply blown up, and perhaps that is why you didn't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mrs. Radovanovic, what is it that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the publication of the statistics administration of the Republic of Croatia, the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ethnic structure per settlement, final results of the population census of Bosnia-Herzegovina linked with the permanent residents of Bosnia, 1940 to 1991, per ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To make it simpler, does this include also the census of 1991, the official ones?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This is the official information of the population census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I will ask you to take a piece of paper and pencil, and I want you to add up something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are now looking at -- I have the book in front of me. This is the document. Page 70 and 71. In English, they are pages 3, 4 [as interpreted]. That is what the translation says. Bosanski Samac, if you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please look at how many -- what is the population of a place called Basik [phoen] in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you look at Domaljevac?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a pencil. You told me to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I want you to take it down and then add it up so that we can put it in the record.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Domaljevac, 4.152.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Grebnice? And I'd like to know the number of Croats, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Grebnice, 1.933 Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please have the table on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think the table could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a moment. Colleagues are correcting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grebnice. Will you please repeat the figure? Place, Grebnice. How many Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about Prud? What is its population?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please add this up if it's not too difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 7.917. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't need this document any more. But I'd also like to tender this, this part of the information into evidence. This is the document that the expert witnesses for the Prosecution used it for their analysis, and I think there will be no problem in admitting it. At the end, we have also Odzak as per village -- population per village, but I do not think it is important. These are merely -- I wanted the Trial Chamber to see what was the ethnic composition of settlements in individual municipalities in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Trial Chamber is of the view is there's no harm in having them on record and in having them admitted since they are showing the figures which the witness has added up, and they have a significance in showing, explaining the faults which she is pointing in the way the Prosecution expert dealt with the figures and the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't understand. Could I -- I would like to tender this document into evidence. May we do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wished to say - perhaps I wasn't clear enough - this source of information, the statistical source of 1991 is the one which was used -- oh, I see. Right. Can we tender into evidence this piece of paper which Mrs. Radovanovic just wrote down. Shall I do it? We need it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just have a sheet of paper so that I can write it down separately because I did it on a document which I need, so I'll need a clean sheet of paper, please, and I'll copy it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D196B/3, and ter for the B/C/S. And the handwritten note will be D196C/3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mrs. Radovanovic, before I come to my final questions, I'd like to invite you to make a brief comment on something. In your analysis, you also touched upon the expert analysis of the Prosecution, and you devoted a special chapter to it. So what I'd like to know is paragraph 56, where you speak about the inaccuracies in distribution of identified persons, and you mention there table 7, the Prosecution's table. Can you please tell us very briefly what is this interesting thing in the distribution of identified persons?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could point out that this also applies to table 13 as well as to table 7, but I mention only table 7. Table 7 in the Prosecution's analysis shows the emigration in Bosanski Samac between 1991 and 1997 and says, I quote: "Table 7 summarises the emigration, that is outmigration, from the prewar municipality of Bosanski Samac." And what does it show us? It shows us emigration from Bosanski Samac between 1991 and 1997. And it is said that two sources were used; one is the population census, and the other one are the electoral rosters, the voters registers of 1997. Now, would you look at the sum total. For this period, 1991 and 1997, 3.339 individuals moved out of Bosanski Samac. However, if you go back to tables 5B and 6B, which the experts show the population out of the country as distributed per newly formed municipalities, 6B and 5B -- sorry, 6B and 5B, you can then see, if you look at them, that from Samac RS, 2.489 people left, that is, they are out of the country. And from Samac, which came under federation, 203 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going slowly. Which means that 2.692 persons moved out. And if we look at table 7, then we get a surplus of 647 individuals. I don't know where this comes from. But since the Prosecution's expert quotes the population census of 1991, and I claim that such information does not exist in the population census of 1991, then we get a difference of 25 per cent, that is, 647 persons emigrated more in 1997 than in all the other tables out of the country which are shown by the Prosecution. And then we can move on and say if these people moved out, left in 1991, then the emigration process followed by the expert is much smaller, that is for this whole period, than the number of persons who emigrated in 1991 alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll ask you some final questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just for the sake of clarity, if we are looking at the table 13, it's page 26 English translation, I think that's a typing error in the first line that this table is related to the year 1977. Obviously, it should be 1997. We have to correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Also, B/C/S version is page 32, the same table, because it was translated from B/C/S where we found this probably typing error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I only have a couple of final questions. Shall we make a break, or perhaps -- but it won't take more than five minutes after the break if we're taking the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic, I have a few final questions. You could answer them briefly as everything is contained in your report, but I would like you to express your official position. In your summary of the results from paragraphs 1 to 8, and in your conclusion under heading 7, you've expressed your main positions with regard to the tasks you were assigned. We don't have to look at those paragraphs mentioned, but I would like to ask you the following question: Are there any sources, demographically speaking, that could be used as reliable sources in relation to the changes in the ethnic structure caused by migration in the territory of the municipalities of Samac and Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There are no official sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, as a professional, as an expert in that field, what would constitute a reliable source that could indicate whether there were changes in the ethnic composition of the population?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: A complete census of the population, and naturally it would be necessary to have all the relevant questions concerning the subject one is interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to the sources, the existing sources that you used, and I'm referring to two key sources, the census and the OSCE voters registers, on the basis of those sources, is it possible to claim when there was migration of the population, if this actually did occur?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, can you answer that question again. It hasn't been correctly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not possible to establish this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When analysing the Prosecution expert's report, in paragraph 6, you stated that the objective assigned -- that the Prosecution's expert had was not attained. Why do you believe that the Prosecution expert's objective was not obtained, was not successfully obtained in the report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I would like to quote the Prosecution's experts, the summary of the results on page 1, and I'll quote: "Our objective is to provide reliable demographic statistical information that provides a basis to evaluate the kind of changes that occurred and the extent of these changes." Such an objective cannot be attained if you do not have reliable sources of information. And it is not possible to obtain such -- to attain such an objective if you want to establish the nature and extent of such migration, and it's not possible to consider these results to be absolutely correct if you don't have reliable sources of information and if the methodology you use is not appropriate, if your approach to the task assigned is not appropriate, then it is absolutely impossible to attain your objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, my name is Di Fazio, I will ask you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution. I hope a few questions. I'd be grateful if you can try to limit your answers and keep them as brief as possible. Dr. Radovanovic, the demographics report of the Office of the Prosecutor concludes at page 24 that the study shows two clear examples of ethnic cleansing which have been shown in the report. Croats and Muslims largely disappeared from Serb Samac and from Serb Odzak --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't follow you. You have to give me the page reference for the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page numbers are not the same. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You're reading out the conclusion of the experts. Is that what you're reading out to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.3. I'll start again. The conclusion of the demographics report of the Office of the Prosecutor is this: "Two clear examples of ethnic cleansing have been shown in this report. Croats and Muslims largely disappeared from Serb Samac and from the Serb Odzak and Vukosavlje municipalities. Based on --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to object to this immediately because the Prosecution expert provided an additional analysis, and in that part, his findings were changed -- her findings were changed, and she said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the addition, the paragraph wasn't mentioned. But I'll read this out in English. [In English] "From Samac RS." [Interpretation] I apologise. I made a mistake. She also added Odzak, Vukosavlje, but it was changed in that they didn't form the majority in Vukosavlje. It was in that respect that her main findings had been modified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll proceed with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You followed that, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I want to stick with my original question, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The Prosecution demographics report concluded that two clear examples of ethnic cleansing have been shown. Croats and Muslims largely disappeared from Serb Samac and from Serb Odzak, Vukosavlje. Based on everything that's contained in your report and everything that you've said today, you, of course, disagree with that conclusion, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. I can say that -- I have to tell you why I don't agree. I don't, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam, I asked you -- if you wouldn't mind. I can assure you that your time here will be a lot shorter short if you just answer my questions as briefly as you can, and Mr. Lukic will clarify anything that remains unclear from my questions, so rest assured that he is there to carry out that task and he will clarify anything that's left unclear and correct any unfairness that may be perceived in the course of my questioning. So you disagree. In your particular report, part 7 of your report, you set out your major conclusions. And at page 28 of the English, and in any event, it's part 7 of your conclusion, the first conclusion that you draw --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The first, under the letter A, is that the radical change in the ethnic structures of federal Samac and the other municipalities studied presented in the expert report of the OTP demographics unit are the consequence of erroneous methodological approaches. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, that's what I stated. That's my claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph C of the three conclusions that you set out, you set out a major finding that by looking at the same territorial framework in 1997 as in 1991, there were no significant changes in ethnic structures in Bosanski Samac and Odzak. Shares of the various ethnic groups in the total population in 1991 and 1997 remain approximately the same. You recall that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The result is, therefore, that you deny that any ethnic cleansing took place in those areas.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing is not a matter I can discuss. I'm a demographer. I can discuss changes in the ethnic composition. I'm claiming here that the ethnic composition was not drastically changed, but this conclusion was reached on the basis of the tables provided by your experts. And if you read -- if you have read the report carefully, this part concerns -- has to do with comments on your experts' findings, and I am claiming that they had tables that they used, but they ignored them, and they didn't reach these conclusions on that basis because they didn't take into account the territorial integrity when examining 1991 and 1997. I can show you these tables in your expert's reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I wish to quote from D2/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam -- Dr. Radovanovic, this is the definition of ethnic cleansing that I am referring to adopted by the Special Rapporteur for the United Nations in his report to the General Assembly Security Council on the 17th of November, 1992. Paragraph 9, page 6: "The term `ethnic cleansing' refers to the elimination by the ethnic group exercising control over a given territory of members of other ethnic groups." That's the -- what I mean when I refer to ethnic cleansing. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've understood that, now that you have said what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. The same rapporteur provided another report on the 28th of August, 1992, if Your Honours please. I'm referring to P161, page 2 of that report. In the course of that report, he commented on the policy of ethnic cleansing, and he said this: "Most of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in particular Bosnia and Herzegovina, is at present the scene of massive and systematic violations of human rights as well as serious grave violations of humanitarian law. Ethnic cleansing is the cause of most such violations." Does that alter your conclusions that you reached in your report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I'm a demographer. My field of interest is demography and population statistics. That doesn't contain the definitions of ethnic cleansing, and a demographer does not deal with such matters. The demographer's task is to demonstrate what the situation is and demonstrate what changes occur. You're a lawyer. I really don't know what the definition of ethnic cleansing is, but if this is the definition you used, the one that you have just read out, then I will believe you. As a demographer, this is not within my field of interest. My task is to be objective and to use information on the basis of which I can demonstrate what the actual situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the course of your study, and in preparing your report, you concluded that there was no large-scale change in the ethnic composition of those relevant territories, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Radical changes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That is inconsistent with there having been any ethnic cleansing having been carried out on those territories, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What are the demographic or political conclusions, well, I can't reach a judgement in that way. What I did, I dealt with two municipalities; the former municipality of Bosanski Samac, and the former integral municipality of Odzak, and I am quite capable of discussing these matters, but what you have read out to me, I can believe you, but I can't discuss radical and nonradical changes of the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Will Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to put a portion of another report, if Your Honours please, to another report presented to the Security Council and dated the 27th of May, 1994, to the witness. This one is not in evidence. I have enough copies to provide to place it in evidence, and it has been disclosed to the Defence. For my purposes, I need not produce it in evidence, however, I'm in a position to do so if you insist, or if you wish me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is a Security Council report, as you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the date is correct, 27th of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 27th of May, 1994. It's -- it carries the identifying number S/1994/674 dated 27th of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're not going to object to a United Nations document. This is a decision for the Trial Chamber, but I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that we received this document half an hour before the beginning of the hearing. I was in contact with Mr. Di Fazio and Mrs. Radovanovic. It was -- Mrs. Radovanovic doesn't know the English language well enough, I translated two paragraphs that were relevant for her, but I would like to inform you of the fact that the entire document has not been translated for the witness. So could questions put to the witness please be framed in such a way that they don't have to do with the contents of the document because it was not possible to present this witness with the translated version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have one paragraph consisting of about eight lines that I wish to put to the witness from the body of the document. That's all. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, provided you read it very slowly so that it's properly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's exactly what I propose to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For our purposes, if we could just have the paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'll provide all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, from the report that I mentioned earlier, I wish to provide you with one paragraph of that report. And if Your Honours please, you will find this at page 34 of the report, and it's paragraph 133 of the report. I'll read it slowly. "The manner in which the policy of ethnic cleansing is carried out by Serbs in Bosnia is consistent throughout a certain geographic area represented by an arc ranging from Northern Bosnia and covering areas in Eastern and Western Bosnia, adjoining the Serb Krajina area in Croatia. The practice of ethnic cleansing is carried out in strategic areas linking Serbia proper with Serb-inhabited areas in Bosnia and Croatia. This strategic factor is significantly relevant to understanding why the policy has been carried out in certain areas and not in others." Now, of course the area that we are concerned with in this case is in the north of Bosnia, and it's in a strategic position because it links Western and Eastern Bosnia. Does the fact that the UN report indicates the carrying out of this policy of ethnic cleansing in this area affect your final conclusions, given that ethnic cleansing, of course, results in population movements?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are, in fact, asking me whether I agree with what you have just read out, although this has nothing to do with demography, nothing at all. I would like to stress the fact that I am a demographer. If I had the opportunity to examine this and saw on the basis of which information this conclusion was reached, I don't know if I would agree with that or not, but at the moment, I can't just agree with you without having any other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. You mentioned the report number and the date. You haven't indicated in the transcript, though, who or which body presented this report to the Security Council. Was it the Special Rapporteur of the earlier report, or was this some other international organisation for states?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will do that now. If Your Honours would just give me a moment, please. Thank you. Your Honours, it's the final report of the Commission of Experts established pursuant to Security Council resolution 780(1992).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One of the defendants who has called you here to give evidence, Mr. Simo Zaric, has written a book called "On The Hague Cross." And in that book, he reproduces an interview that he had with Croatian media. He described ethnic cleansing having taken place in that interview. In the course of that interview with Croatian media, he describes how "not one of the 6.000 Serbs who lived in the municipality - referring to Odzak, of course - remains there now." If you'd had that information prior to preparing your report, would that have affected your conclusions, do you think?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I've heard about this book. But I'm not sure to what extent Mr. Simo Zaric is capable of providing professional evaluation of this. You know, I'm involved in serious matters. Maybe Mr. Simo Zaric mentioned what he saw, what he heard about, but there had to be serious arguments. If I had known that Mr. Simo Zaric had said this, I would not have taken this for granted. I would have tried to find information so that, as a professional, as a scientist, I would have formed an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Simo Zaric is not a professional --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a problem of posing questions related to Mr. Zaric's book, but when talking about this, Mr. Zaric was talking about the process that appeared after the Dayton peace agreement, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I appreciate that Mr. Zaric is not a demographic expert. However, he was a man who lived and operated, carried out his duties and activities, in the area. Isn't the fact that he says that not one of the 6.000 Serbs who lived in Odzak remains there now of significance?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If that is a fact, because I had your expert report which related to the facts that a state institution had issued an OPS, and these facts were not used correctly, they were interpreted in a bad manner. So you would have to define what a fact is, whether it's Mr. Zaric's statement or do you have to have certain arguments to establish what facts are? In general terms, without going into discussing what the facts are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He was -- he arrived in Odzak in July of 1992 and held an important position there. And he was able to describe the fact that there were no Serbs left in Odzak. Now, that's an important fact to take into account, isn't it, in describing population movements?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, are you advising me to use Mr. Simo Zaric as a source of information when addressing the problem of the changed ethnic structure in the municipality of Odzak or Bosanski Samac? If that is so, I must say, this is a very poor source. After all, it is only one statement and only source. I'd need to have more sources if I wanted to be objective and try to present things objectively. And that is my task. Every thinking man should be objective. I do not know whether Mr. Zaric is biased or not biased. I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will have to add a few words. Mr. Zaric said, when he arrived, there were no civilians at all, not just Serbs. He was referring to each -- to all three nationalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that understood, Mr. Di Fazio, the explanation by Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's understood, yes. I don't necessarily accept it, without having an opportunity to go back and read the transcript, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the course of being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, Miroslav Tadic, another defendant in this case, described population movements that occurred in the area of study, Bosanski Samac and Odzak. And he referred to a movement of people in June of 1992 from a village called Srnice involving about 2.000 people, being Serbs, and these people moving into the area of Bosanski Samac and taking up residence in the villages in Bosanski Samac, the villages being Gornji and Donji Hasici, and told the interviewers that those people are still there today, at least as at 1998. And furthermore, that the people who lived in those two villages, namely Croat villages, had left. If that's true, would that affect your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did your expert use these conclusions? If so, then it affected her. But it cannot affect me, a statement of one man, because I do not deal with statements. I deal with numbers, with verifiable figures. In demographic [realtime transcript read in error "democratic"] research, one can [realtime transcript read in error "cannot"] take note of statements, but that is not a common procedure. We're not talking about concepts and do we use this or that? We're talking about whether something changed or didn't. What one man said, if I conducted a questionnaire in Logaco Samac [phoen], and then I heard a thousand people or a hundred people, and so on and so forth, even then I don't know whether I would have taken it into account because this is what people say, and I am not an expert on what people say. I deal with exact sound figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The transcript reads the witness said democratic research; the witness said demographic research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
