utterances.text: That's quite correct, and there's an additional error in the transcript if Your Honours please. The witness did not say line 19 of page 45, "one cannot take note of statements"; the witness said "one can take note of statements but that is not a common procedure."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, let me correct myself. What I said, in demographic research, especially what individuals say, cannot be really taken into account, and then serve as a basis for conclusions. To make a demographic conclusion, I repeat, you must have accurate data, and not basic -- not be influenced by one statement. Besides, I think that the serious professional may not be under the influence of whatever. He must weigh all the possibilities. He must assess all the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If one can take note of statements, even though that may not be a common procedure, reports prepared by offices of the United Nations would be a good and reliable source to use, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not a source. If you have to make a report, you have sources on the basis of which you draw your conclusions. Of course I assume that what the United Nations write, even though I don't know it, is a sort of conclusion that was made. Now, I may accept that conclusion or not accept it, but I have to go through all the elements that underpin it. So I really cannot give you a general answer whether I will respect that or not. But if in that report you have something that deals with Bosanski Samac and Odzak, I'm ready for that, because I studied the matter. But to discuss Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, I really cannot do, especially, and this is intertwined with geostrategic, geopolitical or whatever other positions, because that is not something that I am expert on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object to the question even though we already heard the answer. If the next question goes in the same direction, then if the Prosecutor wants the witness to say whether the United Nations report is based on individual statements, we do not know that from the paragraph that we heard, so the witness is invited to make guesses. But we have to see that this Secretary-General's report is based on statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to leave this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The OTP report, the OTP demographics report, of course, uses two fundamental sources; the 1991 census, and the 1997 and 1998 voters register. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the fundamental is the first one, the census of 1991. We could talk about the other one, whether and how fundamental is it, especially when it comes to demographic research because the population census always was the basis for voters rosters and voters lists could never be used to come to the figure about the census, about the population, especially since when it comes to the methodology, the manner in which data are gathered are completely different. The OSCE lists are based on a voluntary principle, and the second has different methodology and represents one of the major and most important state tasks of any statistical institution. And there are very many other methodological differences. One records the overall population resident permanently in a place where they are recorded, and the others register people who voluntarily apply, so whether they will or will not participate in the elections, not to mention that even in the most advanced countries, you have a number of citizens who never apply to be put on voters lists. Then the population census covers all sorts of features and things and has its purpose and its tasks, and it is based on establishing a total number of the population, distribution, vital statistics, migratory features, and so on and so forth. Voters lists will take only the identification number and the place of residence, or rather, the place where you register for voting and will include only the date of birth and the name. So I do not really see that the two both are fundamental. One of them is but the other one could serve as an aid, but only if it is reliable, if it is trustworthy, and yet once again not for research of such a serious nature as this, and not when it uses such features - and by this, I mean identification numbers and names - which are indecorate, which are unreliable in both sources. So these two features statistically, I mean, in serious statistics and among serious statisticians - and in the first place, I mean the identification number - they are never used, not even in the official statistics. And the name, the first and last name, is something that has never been used as data, as information in any serious statistics. It is taken down during the census simply for easier filing, that is, at the time, they didn't have identification numbers and therefore you used that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, is your answer to my question yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I simply didn't understand. If I said two fundamental, and I say no, they are not both fundamental.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my question has gone right off the screen, but it was a very, very simple question. The OTP report uses two fundamental sources; the census in 1991, and the 1997 and 1998 OSCE voters register. Now, surely you can answer that with a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, I think she has answered that. She had described the other one and also discussed the second source. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In your report, you claim there are no reliable sources to study changes in ethnic composition. If you can possibly, possibly answer the question with a yes or a no, I'd be most grateful. So do you agree that in your report, you claim there are no reliable sources to study changes in ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Di Fazio, could you make a clear reference to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph 1, page 2 of the English report, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, page 2 of the report in the English, I think you'll find it easily in paragraph 1 where you deal with "Summary of Results." Your position is there are no reliable sources. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be preciser, please. Is it my position that there are not reliable sources for 1991 - 1997 period? If that is your question, then I say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, it's the very first sentence of paragraph 1: "In order to conduct an objective expert analysis of changes in the ethnic composition of the population of Bosanski Samac and Odzak in the period after 1991, it's necessary to have valid ethnostatistical data obtained from reliable sources. There are, however, no such sources." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you repeat that criticism in paragraph 10 where you say - and this is page 5, if Your Honours please, of the report - paragraph 10 of your report, midway through the paragraph: "Even if one takes the 1991 census, flawed as it is in terms of the validity of ethnostatistical data as the starting point, ethnostatistical data from the later period are still missing." So you make the point several times that the statistical data relied upon in preparation of the OTP reports was nonexistent or flawed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You ask me questions about what your experts relied on or experts in general? But never mind, I'm saying that such facts, such information, does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You then go on in part 3.1, or part 3 of the report, Sources of Data and Content Related and Methodological Issues and Problems --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me try to follow you. Three point what?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 3.1. It's part 3, or paragraphs 12, 13. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One of the main criticisms that you make of the data used by the OTP demographics unit is subjectivity. You make the observation that answers to questions regarding ethnic affiliation are completely subjective, and you also touched upon this topic earlier today in your examination-in-chief. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In fact, that's a fundamental and major criticism that you make of the census data, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about that characteristic, and I am saying that this characteristic is variable, is changeable, because the criterion for it has not been as firmly established as in some other cases because this criterion is subjective and depends on the changing opinions. And this criterion as a changing one is not something that I will come up with. It has been established a long time ago in all the methodological descriptions of the censuses, it usually says a citizen is free to answer the question about his ethnic origin and nobody may lead it to him or something. We frequently received nonsensical answers because it is very subjective. All depends on how you feel at a given moment or how you sense the situation. You can say whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in fact, you go on to say in paragraph 13, about two-thirds of the way down: "So the statistical picture of the ethnic structure based on census results can be accepted as officially established, but we have to take a critical view of it."

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "This claim is further supported by the fact that data on mother tongue and religion from 1991 were never officially published, and therefore, it's impossible to compare these parameters." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I've lost you because this does not exist in my expert analysis. Yes, please, go back. I don't see it, and therefore I cannot follow. You said para 13, chapter 3. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now tell me -- I really cannot follow you because -- will you please help me. Will you please help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 9 B/C/S, and a sentence begins with words, "U prilog tome ide i..." "This is further supported by the fact..." It is paragraph 13, and about ten lines from the bottom. "This is further supported by the fact..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, I've found it. Thank you. I'm sorry. My apologies. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay, you say that you have to take a critical view of the official statistics, and you go on to say: "This claim is further supported by the fact that data on mother tongue and religion for 1991 were never officially published and therefore it's impossible to compare these parameters." You're saying there, if you did have information about those parameters, it would assist you to help fix the ethnicity of a person who was responding to the questionnaire, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. In this case, in the case of Bosanski Samac and municipality of Odzak, it is of little relevance because they practically speak one and the same language. I'm talking here about the population census as such, and in SFRY, and then you have a situation, since it is ethnically a heterogenous region. Sometimes you have the ethnicity and do not compare with it other characteristics which could be called ethnic features, then you can get a different picture. For instance, I will take Vlachians, who are an ethnic group and who often say they are ethnically affiliated with the milieu they live in. Fine, this is an objection in principle. It does not have to do with Samac, I'm saying generally. When you talk about ethnic features, you cannot choose only one of them, you have to use a number of elements. And in this case, in Bosanski Samac and Odzak, this is irrelevant because they all speak the language they understand, as you call it here, and which is called B/C/S right now. So comparing this, comparing this would not give us a particularly nice result.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, is it the case that you cannot use religion, answers to religion and answers to mother tongue to assist you in fixing identity in the case of Bosanski Samac and Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I've said that neither language nor religion in this expert analysis did not play a single role. You're talking about the general of things; this is about problems of census populations and everything. So in this case, neither religion nor anything else plays a relevant role.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You complain, don't you, that subjectivity affects reliability of people reporting their ethnicity, don't you? You say that's a problem associated with the 1991 census. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Subjectivity means that you can change your position from one census to the other. And if you do, then you must assess that critically. If over ten years period, the number of Yugoslav grows from 10 to 30.000, then this is not demographically explicable. Then this is a subjective decision. Or vice versa, if the number decreases, somebody wanted to be a Yugoslav and later on he didn't want to be a Yugoslav, so it is the subjective position which affects it, and it is in this sense that I spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There are no objective ways for fixing ethnicity. You can't measure the skull of someone or their blood grouping or any other physical characteristics; ethnicity is something that depends upon how a person thinks of themselves. That is so, isn't it, Dr. Radovanovic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is more -- it becomes more objective if you juxtapose two or three characteristics, which perhaps can be ethnically related. And that is for certain. In many countries, you just do not do that. They simply have their nationality. Another thing is your mother tongue. Religion can be a third thing. And then in demography --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Radovanovic, can I just ask you about that last matter that you mentioned, mother tongue. You testified a few moments ago that in Bosanski Samac and Odzak, it couldn't be relevant; they all speak the same language, right? So that's not going to help you in defining ethnicity in that area, in that area of Bosanski Samac and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't have to help me. I'm not defining anything. I'm claiming that there is no absolutely accurate statistical picture about the ethnic composition of those two municipalities, and there is no way we can arrive at it from OSCE lists, and it is taken over from 1991, how can they do it to begin with? Because in view of the issue at hand, between 1991 to 1997, eight years later, somebody, for instance, has opted for a different ethnicity, or saying he didn't belong to any ethnic group. So it has nothing to do with the mother tongue or any other characteristic. You have a source which contains information about ethnicity which has to be dealt critically, and a source which does not include that. But then the Prosecution's expert decide, when we do not have this information, then let's take this and then say that that is the state of affairs in 1997. And that is what I'm objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, the -- you make a fundamental criticism, don't you, in your report of the methodology of the 1991 census because you say the question relating to ethnicity -- or questions relating to ethnicity are subjective. Now, am I correct, yes; or am I incorrect, no?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am treating it critically and say they are subject to changes because they are subjective. But I am not denying the official statistics. I'm merely saying that one needs to approach them cautiously and that it is very risky to take them over and accept them after such a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Given the ethnic tensions that existed in the early 1990s in Yugoslavia, would that not be a factor that would cause people to identify strongly with a particular group?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise? I don't really understand what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Given the ethnic tensions that existed in the early 1990s in the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia, would that be a factor that would cause people to identify more strongly with a particular grouping, not being Yugoslav? So for example, Croat, Muslim, or Serb?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the ethnic classification in the statistics of the former Yugoslavia and therefore in Bosnia-Herzegovina includes 32 different options. You have 18 or 17 possibilities. You have peoples, national minorities, ethnic groups, and so on and so forth. You can say that you are affiliated, to opt for a regional affiliation, and you can refuse to answer it. So when I say regional affiliation, I say I'm a Sarajevan, I'm a Belgrader, a Krajinian, that could also be an answer to the question about ethnic affiliation. So in addition to Yugoslavs, you had a number of other options. You could say whatever. You could say -- you could say anything. So that it varied from one census to another, and whether it had a role, well -- I'm sorry. And that is why there is the category called "other." So when the information about the ethnic composition is demonstrated and one doesn't use very broad classifications, because in Bosnia-Herzegovina and other areas, you don't have only Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. They have Jews, and Roma and Germans. Now, the share of each of these groups, of course, is another matter. Turks, and many other ethnic communities. So that all that is under "other". When you present the chief result in the census publications, then you select ethnic communities based on their share. But if you go to the administration, then you will find the background material, well, you would find 39 different ethnic options. And this is this very broad national classification. But such a broad national classification is very difficult to show in published census results, then you usually get only most numerous ethnic communities, and all the other figures, all the other findings, are kept in the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You agree, don't you, that the object of the OTP study, demographics unit, was to reconstruct the 1991 population and its ethnic composition and then look at that same population in 1997, using the OSCE voters register. Now, please, please do not tell us whether you consider they achieved that, or mistakes they may have done in carrying that out, but that was their object.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me to confirm what the objective of your experts was. Well, they wrote down that these were -- this was reliable information, reliable demographic information. That's their objective. Am I supposed to confirm their objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me revise the question. I put it to you - do you agree - that the object of the study conducted by the OTP demographics unit was to reconstruct the 1991 population and its ethnic composition, and then look at that same population in 1997, using the OSCE -- 1997 and 1998, using the OSCE voters register. And do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you define this precisely. We know what the objective of your experts was. I don't agree that they carried out their work correctly. The reconstruction of population was totally erroneous, and the matching was not correct either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Madam Radovanovic, if you know what the objective of the Prosecution experts was, you can answer my question. My question is this: The objective of the Prosecution experts was to study, to reconstruct the 1991 population and its ethnic composition, and then look at that same population, using the 1997/1998 OSCE voters register. Agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't agree because they wrote down what their objective was, and you are rephrasing it. They said: "Our objective is to provide reliable demographic and statistical information which provides a basis to assess the kind of changes and the extent." It didn't say that their objective was to reconstruct the population and to make a comparison, so there is a significant difference between these two objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you agree that the objective of the OTP study was to study the movement of people who in 1991 gave themselves the tag of Croat or Muslim or Serb, or that at least that was one of its objectives?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If that was their conception, well, I don't know about that, but this isn't something that they wrote down. They didn't say that they would be examining the movement. There was nothing we could discuss on the basis of maps, but I have never seen anything in the course of my professional career. They said their objective was to provide their opinion, provide their professional findings about the changes that occurred in the ethnic composition. They mentioned that this was their objective in the municipalities of Odzak and Bosanski Samac in 1991 and 1997, and then they quite explicitly stated what their objective was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You would agree, don't you -- you would agree, wouldn't you, that the OSCE voters register for 1997 and 1998 provided no information as to ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the only way that movements of people between 1991 and 1997 can be achieved is by looking at the tag they gave themselves in 1991 in the census. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise. I don't understand you at all. What do you mean by "movement of the population"? Migration or movement in the changes to the ethnic composition? And what do you mean when you say what they assigned to themselves, the tag they gave themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I mean movement in and out of the municipalities. And by the tag that they gave themselves, I mean the answer that they provided in the census questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought you -- when you talked of the tag, I thought you meant the ethnicity they choose for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Your Honour is quite correct. Perhaps I should rephrase my question. The answer they provided in the census questionnaire as to their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please clarify the question, because after all these interventions, I'm no longer sure as to what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Because the OSCE voters registers provided no information as to ethnicity, if you want to study movements of people within the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Odzak and without, and going out of the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Odzak, the only way to do that is by ascertaining the tag they gave themselves in 1991 in the census questionnaire; that is, how they described themselves; as a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't understand you. You're asking me if the OSCE monitors the movement, but they don't do that. They have a list of the registered voters. And the only way is for those voters to take the national declaration from 1991, to base themselves on the national declaration, what they declared themselves to be in 1991. OSCE doesn't follow, doesn't monitor any kind of movement, they just register the voters in the three municipalities. They don't monitor movement of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But if you want to see what happened to people who answered the questionnaire in 1991, you can use the voters register to see where they were in 1997. Correct? That is, by reference to the municipality in which they register to vote. And so if a Serb answered the questionnaire in 1991 saying he's a Serb, you can use the OSCE voters register to see where that person is in 1997, regardless of whether or not he has changed his mind as to whether he's a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can't use it for the simple reason that the electoral lists don't contain references to the nationality of the individuals. You have to answer what your name is, you have to provide your personal identification number, mention the municipality in which you are registered, and there is other information that has to be provided. So it is by no means possible to make a comparison, to say whether a Serb or someone in 1991 said the same in 1997, because such information is simply not available. According to the methodology followed by your experts, you can adopt this, you can take this over and say a Serb from 1997 is a Serb from 1997, and I can agree with you that in 90 per cent of the cases, that might be true. But what to do when you erroneously match up a Serb, or rather, when the personal identification number and the name is not correct, when you carry out the matching up process on the basis of initials, and then someone who was perhaps a Croat or a Muslim, you claim - I don't know on the basis of what information - you claim that someone was a Muslim or a Serb or a Croat. And that is where the problem lies. I'm not wondering -- I'm not addressing the issue as to whether what was stated in 1991 is correct or not. The methodology used, especially if you use the first and last name, this is not relevant information. You saw that in Odzak there were identical names for various individuals. There was a lot of -- a lot of personal identification numbers were duplicated. Many names and surnames were duplicated. There were many illegible names and last names. If the personal identification number is not valid, then one uses the initials to match it up with someone else. How many times do the letters SR appear? What do you think? So the first SR that I come across, if I think that this is the correct SR, then I attribute the nationality that I found in some list. And I think that this methodology is not correct. And whether the nationality is a hundred per cent correct or not, I won't discuss this. I'm just talking about the possibility that in the case of some individuals, they might have -- some individuals who might have declared themselves to be of another nationality, in such cases, they were probably described as something that they weren't. I would like to see the information from 1997. I would like to see how many Yugoslavs there are now in Samac and in Odzak. And I'd like to see what the figure is, what the declarations of nationality would be like. So adopting this information, taking over this information, is methodologically not a valid procedure because you are comparing and matching up bad information with bad information and You are trying to obtain good results.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. In the last answer of Dr. Radovanovic, it's the last passage, page 61, line 13 until line 22, Dr. Radovanovic mentioned that it should be "and we all expecting a new censuses in the coming years." So maybe that will be important for the understanding of the explanation because it is not in the transcript due to the fast explanation of Dr. Radovanovic. And I kindly ask her to slow down a bit because of the interpreters' efforts to precisely translate what was said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it your position that you can't use the 1991 census to provide accurate analysis of ethnic composition in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, my position is that you can't use OSCE lists together with characteristics that are not correct in the 1991 census. I'm not contesting the census; I am contesting certain characteristics provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You agree, don't you, in your report that you complain about features of the 1991 census, for example, the topic that we just spent the last half an hour talking about, subjectivity. Another example that you use in your report are the problems with scanning. These are fundamental problems. They would lead the Trial Chamber to conclude, wouldn't they, those matters that you raise in your report, that you can't use the 1991 census to provide reliable figures for ethnic distribution or composition in the former Yugoslavia? Otherwise, why on earth did you spend all that time in your reports making those observations?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said. You're putting words in my mouth. I said that the characteristic -- the national characteristic, whenever you're doing anything, whether you're using information from any census, not only that of 1991, when using such information, you have to have a very critical and cautious approach. I'm not denying or contesting anything. But you know if you're a serious expert and professional, you just -- you don't just base yourself on such characteristics, but you make comparisons from that same census. This is not a matter I'm contesting. I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that this has to be used cautiously or, rather, such information cannot simply be adopted seven years later. And on the basis of that information, you cannot then claim we have reached these findings. With regard to this matter, I have written several articles about this, and this is the criticism of the methodology used in obtaining information on nationality. Ethnostatistical information. So this is not a matter of contesting of the validity of the census; it's a matter of drawing attention to the fact that if you are a serious scientist, you have to be very cautious when weighing up the information, and especially when taking over information, when adopting information after so much time has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you, and I'm asking you about the 1991 census. Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber: Paragraph 20: "In the 1991 census, personal identification numbers and first and last names were optically read for the first time. But this was not checked, and so this data is considered statistically useless because there are too many errors." Now, you told the Trial Chamber how it is that if the scanning process produced data that is statistically useless, how does that translate into your saying that you can use this 1991 census in studies relating to ethnic composition? Tell the Chamber what "statistically useless" means, please.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about the personal identification numbers. Well, in all censuses, and in all types of statistics, you have information that is reliable and information that is less reliable. This is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: With respect, I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking to you explain to the Trial Chamber what you mean when you say that "in the 1991 census, personal identification and first and last names were optically read for the first time, but this wasn't checked so this data is considered statistically useless." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It means that they contained a lot of errors. But this is just one of the characteristics of the census, and it was introduced for the first time on that occasion. And this doesn't mean that if one characteristic is erroneous, that the census is not valid. If you have 30 or 40 or 50 per cent of errors in statistical terms, you can't claim that this information is reliable. This was demonstrated in the case of Samac and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, if the census can't give you accurate information relating to the name of a person or their identification, that's a pretty serious criticism, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't. The first and last name was never an essential part of the census in terms of processing information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You, of course, have used the 1991 census in your own articles and studies, haven't you, apart from this particular study that you're discussing now?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in fact, you used the 1991 census as a source in your article entitled "Demographic Growth and Ethnodemographic Changes in the Republic of Serbia" didn't you, published in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I know that you don't have the B/C/S version of that article, but it's obtainable, isn't it, on the internet from the internet library of Serb culture. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. I wasn't aware of the fact that it was on the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And its source is "Serbian Question in the Balkans, University of Belgrade publisher, faculty of geography, Belgrade, 1995." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd just like to read to you the introduction to that article that you wrote. "Complex processes in the ethnodemographic growth in the Republic of Serbia could be continuously followed only from the time when regular statistical research was organised. The most important statistical data are the data on the natural movements of population and the censuses. In today's Republic of Serbia, censuses were conducted at irregular intervals and in differing historical circumstances. So an abundance of data derived from 36 population censuses in the period 1934 to 1991 (18 Serbian, 5 Austro-Hungarian, 5 Bulgarian, and 8 Yugoslav) though with different degrees of reliability, non-uniform identifications, and incomparability and scope, still present a valuable source of information which we will use by applying ethnostatistics to briefly demonstrate the population growth, ethnic structure, and changes in the ethnic structure of the population in Serbia. The censuses in Yugoslavia after World War II offered very meager ethnostatistical data of restrictive distribution. Precise questions on the basis of which conclusions about the ethnic structure of the population in Serbia could be made were asked for the first time in the 1948 census. Some of the earlier censuses contained only the information on religion or the data both on religion and native language, which offered rather ambiguous results for the population in the territory of today's Serbia." You felt confident, didn't you, in using the 1991 census to study ethnic structure and changes in ethnic structure in Serbia, didn't you? And I'm sure you can answer that, I think, with a yes or a no. Did you feel confident in using the 1991 census to study ethnic structure and changes in ethnic structure in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I used that, but you didn't read everything. First of all, this is an excerpt from another article that was published at the faculty of geography, and in a book called "The Ethnic Territory of the Serbs" and that contains a criticism of the methodology of obtaining information, statistical information. And if you read on, you'll see that when I say real information, et cetera, I put that in inverted commas, real information on the national composition. But I conclude that this is our reality, this is the situation we are facing, and this is what we will have to use. So I'm not at all contesting the census, and I'm not contesting the issue of nationality. All I am saying is that it is necessary to be cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: You would agree, wouldn't you --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I haven't answered your question. You said that I used the census. I did. But eight years later, I didn't give anyone from that census the same description. This is the state at a given point in time, and whether someone likes this or not, that's the way it is. It's official state information. I wouldn't dare to get involved in foreseeing what the case would be in five, seven, or ten years' time. I wouldn't dare attribute to give an individual something that that person stated six or seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise again. Just in order to have a clear transcript, page 65, line 22, instead of year 1934, it should be 1834. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Actually, that's the year I heard, 1834.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, 1834, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is there any reason why the 1991 census is not -- let me rephrase that. You would agree, wouldn't you, given your answer, that the 1991 census is a valuable source of information that you can use to demonstrate ethnic structure and changes in ethnic structure in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The census is the official source that we will use for information on the national composition. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try and turn to another topic, Dr. Radovanovic, and again, if you could possibly answer questions briefly, it would benefit us both, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What time do Your Honours wish to break? Would now be an appropriate moment? I'm leading to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think we have two minutes. You say you want to start another topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can break now and continue at 18.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Dr. Radovanovic, essentially your position is this, in paragraph 20 of your report: "The 1991 census provides names and identity numbers which were read optically and not checked." And you say this data is considered statistically useless because there are too many errors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This is also referred to in your report as the process of substitution.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Process of substitution is something else. But some of the problems are due to substitution, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you a document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if Your Honours please, can we very briefly go into closed session because this contains confidential material, people's names --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, private session. The document I'm about to show to the witness has already been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One of -- your position is, isn't it, that because of the census -- because the census material may contain mistakes in name and ID numbers, one cannot match the 1991 census material with the OSCE material. That's one of the problems, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they can be matched, but not in a relevant way because you're automatically excluding a large percentage of the population. 40 per cent in Samac, 36 per cent in Odzak who cannot be matched because their personal identification numbers are not correct and perhaps their names are not correct. And you are simply disregarding them, and that is not a small percentage. Even if they live there in 1991, and perhaps in 1997, in the same territory, you simply deny them the possibility of being matched, represented, included, and having them contributing to a more reliable information. It is a highly selective approach. And you say, well, now I've matched it, right, so that's it. It's not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraphs 24 and 25 of your report, you talk about this problem of data coupling or matching, don't you? 24 and 25. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You make the complaint, or you make the observation, I should say, that in the 1991 census in Odzak and Bosanski Samac, there are a surprisingly large number of identical first names, father's names, and last names. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you came up with 1500, approximately, pairs of identical first and last names. And in Odzak, approximately 589 -- well, 589 persons had the same first name, father's name, and last name. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You got those figures, didn't you, from your study of material provided to you some time ago, some weeks ago, by the office of the demographics unit? You studied the material and you came up with those figures, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did. And if you'd like me, I can illustrate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just answer the question. And I might add, too, Dr. Radovanovic, that the Prosecution entirely agrees with those figures that you have reached. You're quite correct, you're quite correct, that there were 1562 pairs of essentially same names, and 589 similar cases relating to Odzak. However, when you add the year of birth to those names and compare them, would it have the effect of reducing those matches?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I've found a large number of pairs that are absolutely identical identification number. I didn't take out only the names, but also the identification numbers. And I told you that it is unique, I mean, there are not two, so I took out pairs who have the same first name, the same last name, and the same personal identification number, and also those with same first and last names but different identification numbers. So, sir, I'm not talking only about the identical first and last names, but also identical identification numbers. Now, your experts used the years of birth. I can quote you strings of people with the same names and same year of birth. And also people with different names and identical identification numbers, which is impossible because that number is unique. Names can, of course, be -- there can be many same names, but your expert says that it is really seldom that in one territory one finds persons with first -- with the same first and last names and the same identification numbers. And I can quote it even here. But I'm showing you the opposite. Not only that it is not -- does not happen seldom, but traditionally speaking, in our country, or in our former country, in Yugoslavia, you come frequently across the first and the last names because grandchildren are often given their grandparent's name; a son will get his grandfather's name or a daughter a grandmother's name so that is not a rare occurrence. And your expert says -- he says, I'm quoting page 6 of the B/C/S version of the expertise of your people. It is very unusual for two different persons to have -- to bear identical names and to have been born on an identical date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So is it the case that --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Our research shows the opposite. So that it is not an exception. It is not exceptionally rare for people to have the same first and last names, and to have been born on the same dates, and there are examples which I can quote. But I also have to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We agree. It's very common, isn't it, for people in those areas, very common, very common indeed, for people in those areas to have the same surname, for fathers to hand on their names to their sons, for a lot of people to have the same name, surname and first name. It's part of the naming tradition in that area, isn't it, so you really run into a lot of people with the same name, don't you? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, if you add the year of birth as another variable and compare these names, would you expect the number of matching pairs to reduce? Would you expect that to take place?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you define what you mean by reduction? If you find ten out of a thousand cases, is that -- does that mean that it has been reduced? If your sample is bad, if you have a small sample which is not representative, well, in that case, you have to define what it means to say that the number is reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If you compare, if you analyse the 1.562 people with identical first names, father's names and last name, and then add another variable, being their year of birth, would you expect that number of 1.562 to be reduced? Say, for example, to an order of around a hundred or perhaps 92, in particular. Would you expect that? Would that sort of result surprise you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would expect the number to be reduced, but I wouldn't start speculating as to the order by which it would be reduced because I haven't had the opportunity to check this and to claim that it would be reduced to the figure of 90. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You know, don't you, that by adding variables, something as simple as the year of birth, when you're analysing people who have got the same name, first name, father's name, and surname, when you add something as simple as the year of birth, you really reduce, and drastically reduce, the number of matches, don't you? And I can tell you, and I put it to you, that in fact, that's what our OTP demographics expert did, and he came up with a figure of 92 matches in Samac, and 26 for Odzak. And that is, in fact, 46 pairs of people who have been recorded twice, or 13 pairs of people who have been recorded twice out of a population of about 30.000 for each of those municipalities of Odzak and Bosanski Samac. What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My comment is that I really don't know what the figure would be. But if I have the names in front of me and the year of birth, and if I asked myself whether out of 1.568, whether out of that number, one would obtain this result --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you know, don't you, that by introducing more variables, as the OTP demographics team did in their report, you can really reduce that number of matches, those sorts of numbers of false matches. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you have the full name, I assume that this would be possible. But this is guesswork, and I don't like guessing. But your experts, on page 6 of the B/C/S version, heading 2.4, said the following, and I quote: "For people who have not been matched in the first round, we gradually extended the criteria for search for one or two orders of change. For example, including the year but not the full date. By including the first letter of [realtime transcript read in error "or"] the first and last name." Only the years without the date and the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you know also don't you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We have something here in the transcript. The answer that our expert gave was "by including the first letter of the first and last name." Not "or the first and last name," because the way it is now in the transcript would suggest that the full first and last name was one of the criteria. And the witness said that it was just first letter of the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. That's probably right. In fact, I'll put to you what I have in the -- what I have in the OTP demographics report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: "Consequently, for persons not matched in the first round we made the search criteria gradually broader for one or more variables, for example by only including the year and not the full date of birth, or only the initial of the first name in addition to the surname. The results of such matches have, however, to be inspected visually to decide if the matches are more likely to be the same person or not, by looking at other available information, such as municipality, place of birth, or residence. For example, the place of birth may be given as a municipality on one list and a small hamlet located in the municipality on the other list. It would be very complicated, if possible at all, to automate such checks. For difficult cases, we checked the 1991 census for additional information; for example, information about family members of the person in question." So your complaint - I wouldn't say it's a complaint - your observation that there are 1500, thereabouts, matching pairs for Samac, and I think about 800 or so matching pairs for Odzak, is really not the full picture at all, is it, because you can use other variables to reduce that and reduce it drastically.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It would be intellectually honest if your expert had said how many cases had been matched in the first round and how many matches had been found in the second round, and I would then be able to adopt a position. But in statistical terms, this first phase of matching on the basis of the personal identification number is really important, and here this was not done very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But the Trial Chamber can be satisfied, can't it, that according to the face of the report anyway, the OTP demographics report, that a lot of -- more than one or two variables were used and, in difficult cases, visual inspection of the records was conducted.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're wrong there, too. In difficult cases, in my opinion, contain the initials and the year of birth. That is what your expert has mentioned. "SR, 49, Bosanski Samac." How is your expert going to know who and what SR is, if the expert find, let's say, just 50 such SRs, what is the ethnic affiliation of this person SR?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I think I would like to move on rapidly, if I may, to the last issue that I want to ask you about, and that's the final conclusions reached in both the OTP demographics report and your report. You said -- sorry. In your report, you make it clear that you observed no significant changes to the ethnic composition of the territory of Bosanski Samac and Odzak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's what it says in the conclusion, but that is not what I stated in my report. That is a criticism and a comment on your experts' report. I said in the summary - it's item 4 - given everything mentioned above, we conclude that by comparing and combining statistical information obtained from the regular census of 1991, and from the electoral lists of 1997 and 1998, it is not possible to carry out a statistical and demographic analysis that would be -- that would objectively demonstrate the changes to the ethnic composition of the population in the territory of the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Odzak. And this conclusion that follows the heading containing comments on your experts' report has to do with the fact that I commented on what had been done. And it has to do with why this last conclusion in -- under C in your experts' table, I said that your experts had this table, but I stated that I do not know why they did not take it into account. I'll provide you with the reference now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's okay. Could I just ask you to look, please, at your report, because I must confess I'm having some trouble understanding your answer. It's in the English at page 28, if Your Honours please. And in your report, it's headed VII "Conclusion," c-o-n-c-l-u-s-i-o-n. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Chapter 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Chapter 7, yeah. Could you just read out, please, what you have at the top there, please. Read it into the transcript, chapter 7, and then the word next to it. What word is there, so the interpreters may --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your report. Your report. Your B/C/S report, chapter 7, VII, and then there's a word next to that. In English it comes out as "conclusion." What is it --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't see the transcript here, but it's not important. Chapter 7, conclusion, under A: "The radical change --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just ask you one other question. "Conclusion," that's your -- your conclusion, isn't it? You wrote this report, and you prepared it, so that's your conclusion, isn't it? Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's my conclusion, but please bear in mind that it refers to what your experts did. So my conclusion, well, yes, I will accept that it is mine, if that's important, and if you allow me to read it out. It has to do with what was claimed by your experts, and I do agree that they had a look at the tables and that this relates to conclusion C.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And your conclusion, your conclusion, in part C, under chapter VII of your report, is this: "Looking at the same territorial framework in 1997 as in 1991, there were no significant changes in the ethnic structures of Bosanski Samac and Odzak. The shares of various ethnic groups in the total population in 1991 and 1997 are approximately the same." Now, it is rare to see such plain, simple, and obvious language. That's your conclusion, isn't it? You'd have to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you would agree, wouldn't you, that without going into huge amounts of detail, that essentially the conclusion of the OTP demographics unit was that if you study the territory, territory of the post-Dayton -- the post-Dayton four municipalities that were carved out of Bosanski Samac and Odzak, you end up with a preponderance of Serbs in some of them and a preponderance of Croats and Muslims in others. In other words, in Serb Odzak, there is an overwhelming majority of Serbs; and in federation Odzak, there are an overwhelming majority of Muslims and Croats. And the same applies in Bosanski Samac. In Republika Srpska Samac, the vast majority are Serbs; and in Domaljevac Samac, the vast majority are Croats. That's essentially -- whether they are right or wrong, but that's essentially their conclusion. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. That is their conclusion, but the conclusion that they reached was reached on the basis of erroneous information because if you are discussing Muslims in federal Odzak, there are no Muslims in RS Odzak. As the villages were divided, these Muslims are in the same place; in the same house, the same street. They did not move all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment on the accuracy. I understand that you challenge that. Please understand I understand your position. You're not happy with their methodology. I understand that perfectly well. But that essentially is the difference in the two major conclusions reached in your report and in their report, in the OTP demographics unit. Correct? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've understood your question. Do I agree with their methodology? If the methodology is incorrect, the conclusion cannot be correct. Do I agree with their conclusion? No, I don't. The differences between our conclusions are the result of the application of different methodologies, a good methodology and a bad one, if you're asking me this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll start again, Dr. Radovanovic. Let's see if we can, if possible, scoot home to a nice finish before 7.00, okay? If we can possibly do that, that would be good. Essentially, the conclusion of the OTP demographics unit is that of the four municipalities that were carved out of Bosanski Samac and Odzak, the former 1991 municipalities, ethnic preponderances or majorities are to be seen, namely a lot more Serbs, the overwhelming majority of Serbs in Republika Srpska Samac, a lot more Croats in Domaljevac Samac, a lot more Serbs in Odzak Vukosavlje, and a lot more Croats and Muslims in federation Odzak. That essentially is their conclusion. Now, I'm not asking you if it's right or wrong, but that's essentially their conclusion, so that Their Honours know and it's clear.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That not is the essence of their conclusion. You have paraphrased their conclusion, which is very brief. I could read it out. I'll quote the Prosecution's expert reports: "To conclude, we can say -- summing up, two clear examples of ethnic cleansing have been shown in this report. Croats and Muslims largely disappeared from the Serb Samac, and from the Serb Odzak Vukosavlje. Before the war in both these areas, Croats and Muslims represented a considerable fraction of the actual population." That is the conclusion that is not correct and it is a conclusion that I contest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks, that's fine. That's just fine. Thank you very much for pointing it out. That's from the addendum to the report that was initially provided, correct, the addendum report that the Prosecution OTP demographics unit provided?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not an addition. This is what appears in the conclusion of the Prosecution's expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at this document that I produce to you. In fact, these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, copies have been provided to the Defence, served on the Defence. I have copies here for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at what I describe as the more colourful map headed with the English words - I hope that you can identify it - "Ethnical Majority Recently." I know you don't read English, but on the bottom left-hand corner of that document, there are the words "Sources, present population, UNHCR, September 1999." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And it -- the colouring code, I'll assist you on that, it's very, very simple for our purposes, exceptionally simple. The brightest red refers to Serb over 66 per cent, and the darkest blue refers to Croat over 66 per cent. So you can see that very, very easily because we're just going up to the top of Northern Bosnia, and you can see the municipalities up there. You can see that Odzak, federation Odzak, is blue, all blue, and that indicates at least 66 per cent Croats in that particular municipality. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And underneath, and although it's in small writing, you can Vukosavlje, and that, of course, is Serb Odzak, and that's all in red, so that indicates Serb population of over 66 per cent. Do you see that? And essentially, the same applies to the next-door municipality, Samac and Domaljevac Samac. Do you see that? Essentially the red and the blue. It's very clear. Those figures on the face of this document obtained from the UNHCR in September of 1999 tend very much to suggest majority Croat populations in Odzak federation and Domaljevac Samac, and majority Serb populations in Vukosavlje and RS Samac, don't they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is the position of the IMG company. You can see in the lower right-hand corner, it says that it is a map, a sort of guiding map, an orientation map. It doesn't say that it is founded on a scientific basis. I'm just assuming - this is guesswork again - that this involves estimates. I don't know what the basis for these estimates is. This may be acceptable for media purposes, but in professional terms, I'd be very cautious in accepting this because they themselves emphasise the fact that this map is not to be taken as necessarily representing IMG views. It just says it's a sort of guiding map. It's the position of the company that probably based itself on some of the UNHCR estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic assisted you in studying this map, didn't he, and he translated bits of it to you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic provided me with this map and translated parts of it because I insisted that he do so. I don't know English, and I wasn't provided with the Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Of course, I understand that, and I understand the difficulty that you're labouring under, and I'm not trying to take advantage of that by any means. But it says that the map is not to be taken as necessarily representing IMG views on boundaries or political status. If the International Management Group used UNHCR figures from September of 1999, and if those figures are reliable or reasonably reliable, they suggest, don't they, ethnic preponderances in those municipalities in the way that I've described to you in my earlier question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the question is asking the witness to speculate. What could the organisation IMG have concluded on that basis? But apart from the map, we don't see how this was compiled, we don't know about the sources. I think that the expert is being asked to speculate on what the organisation, what the company wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, maybe my learned friend can give us a little more details about the background of this IMG company, because after our research, the IMG is the world's largest, most diverse and only truly global company dedicated to the marketing and management of sport, leisure and lifestyle and so on. I don't know if we are speaking of the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: My understanding -- but of course this is only from the bar table my understanding is that it is the organisation responsible for handling reconstruction from war damage in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the more important point is the one mentioned by Mr. Lukic where he says it is not known on what they based the information on, their sources, their data, to come to this conclusion which is shown on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. I'd ask that the document be marked for identification at this stage. And its sources -- and in addition, I also note that the document does go some way to answering that question, present population, UNHCR, September 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Her Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Sorry. It does say that, but what I'm saying is how they came to compile these population figures, what methodology they used, what sources of information they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If Your Honours please, can I ask that the document simply be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't object to having this document marked for identification, but it will really be a serious problem if the Prosecution subsequently provides some evidence with regard to this matter. Our expert will then have to express a position on this analysis. That's what the Prosecution wanted from the expert. The expert will leave, and if the Prosecution subsequently provides documents without having had the expert express an opinion, then the Trial Chamber will have to assess the validity of such a document in a special way. I appreciate the fact that my learned colleague didn't know when the expert would be. We got these maps over the weekend. We tried to find something about these sources. Mrs. Radovanovic herself couldn't find some information, and we were really at a disadvantage. If we get these maps and we don't have other information, I think we'll have problems. But I don't object to marking them for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to do that in respect of the second document as well, if Your Honours, please, and that will then, I think, complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So which one do you call the first one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: "Ethnical majority recently," and the second one is the "ethnical breakdown recently." I would ask that the number be ascribed so I can finish this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map on ethnical majority will be treated as Document P184 ID. And the map on ethnical breakdown will be treated as Document P184A ID. I apologise, P183. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In fact, I have no further questions because that document speaks for itself, and any later use of it we will sort out later. So that, in fact, completes my cross-examination, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the re-examination will begin tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber that I only had two questions. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has any questions, but I have two fairly short questions. We know that the interpreters have had a difficult day today, but if they would agree to carry on for ten minutes, unless the Trial Chamber thinks that there will be more questions, then of course I will accept your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber would like to ask the interpreters to bear with us so that we can complete this expert witness since the re-examination will be very brief, and perhaps one question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I should also like to thank the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Radovanovic, in the very beginning of the cross-examination, the Prosecutor did not allow you to explain why you disagreed with their analysis, so this would be my first question, why you disagree with the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why do you disagree with the Prosecution's claim that we are dealing with a co-national form of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because the Prosecutor says that on the basis of the conclusions of their experts. And I claim under full responsibility that the Prosecutor's team used very deficient statistical data, and on the basis of deficient statistical data, you cannot come to a correct decision. Why are they deficient? They are deficient regarding the structural population because they simply exempted a large number of the population of 1991 and disregarded completely. It is also deficient because they are not considering the identical territorial entity, and because they do not know what is the territorial entity, we get a misrepresentation, and it is a misrepresentation because it is due either to the administrative subdivision or statistical errors. For instance, if we have a look at this, for instance, Odzak. Odzak, yellow here represents settlements which were exempted from survey-tion [as interpreted] because the Dayton boundary goes through them, so they say we shall exclude this population. But what that means is that you're excluding a complete Muslim population concentrated only in the settlement of Odzak. It is this here. This is the municipality made of different settlements. Now, what happened in the elections in 1997? I'm sorry so sorry. Since the Dayton boundary goes through these places, when registering for voting, you are bound to register according to the new municipal code and say, "I now live in federal Odzak," which is number 20, or in Odzak which belongs to Republika Srpska, which is number 19. So this settlement and the population there, owing to the statistical code and the Dayton boundary, is split into federal and RS Odzak. The population - and we are interested in Muslims here - who live in the settlement of Odzak, in the same house, on the same street, when they go to vote, give a new code, and then it turns out, because that part where they are registering is in federal Odzak, that in federal Odzak, according to the Prosecution's analysis, a certain number, and we can forget whether the figure is accurate or not, but that we have there a certain number of Muslims, and in Odzak, which is in Republika Srpska, these Muslims do not exist. And on the basis of that, a conclusion is made that in Serb Odzak, ethnic cleansing has taken place, but that is not accurate. They were not there. I mean, their house, their street was not in that part. They were not there in 1991. So they all stayed where they were, but they have been split by a statistical code that is the Dayton boundary. And on the other hand - and I think this is a good example - the Prosecution's experts disregard the principle of settlements and show even the direction of migrations, and say from Samac RS, Republika Srpska, Croats were expelled. Disregarding, ignoring that a whole settlement, which is Prud, has administratively been relocated from Samac and annexed to the municipality of Odzak. So all those Croats who come to register to vote say they are Croats from federal Odzak. They have all stayed in their homes in the same settlement. They have not moved anywhere. I mean, all, I mean I don't mean all down to the last one, but I'm saying that this is the population which has not migrated. They migrated by a statistical code, the whole settlement. And the Prosecution expert gives the migration routes and say Croats from Samac, disregarding the settlement of Prud or those which are divided and which with population in Samac, you have two, for instance, Croat settlements and one where Croats are predominant. I'm sorry, I was showing you Samac and spoke about Odzak, but you understand what I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is clear that yellow means settlements which were split?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This question arises from Prosecution's question when they asked you about the matching methodologies and what they used in addition to personal identification numbers and mother tongues and all the rest in view of the scanning. Will you please look at paragraphs 28 and 29 of your report, and in that report, you say first that on the basis of your matching principle, you only used the principle of identification numbers, that is, you didn't use the broad methodology used by the Prosecution. That is what you say in paragraph 28. And then you show how many you managed to match. And what does the paragraph 29 say? Is there a significant difference between your matching strictly only PINs, that is personal identification numbers, and what the Prosecution did, and could this produce then a discrepancy in results obtained?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we have a discrepancy because we obtained completely different numbers for Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, but statistically speaking we found 37 per cent matched numbers, and the Prosecution's witness, 40. So there is a difference in conclusion. If you observe a correct principle, a correct methodology, there shouldn't be such discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you're only matched personal identification numbers to get 37 per cent matched, and the Prosecution, by using some other methods, to obtain 40-odd percentages matched?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Radovanovic, I have only one question. I know that you don't like to make guesses. You are only interested in valid scientific research. But let us for a moment assume that the data you had from the year 1991, from the census, and the data you had from the voters list in 1997 were correct in all respects, and that you used them in a scientifically valid manner to compare what was the situation in 1991 and in 1997. How much does it tell us about what was the situation and the movements of people from one place to another in the years 1992, 1993, and 1994? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only if you have accurate data for 1991 and 1997, you cannot -- and I claim it under full responsibility. You cannot learn what went on in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Radovanovic. We have finished. You may leave the courtroom. Before we rise, there's one matter the Trial Chamber would like to deal with. The witness can be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we can start. This is a matter concerning the decision of the Appeals Chamber regarding the cross-examination and refreshing memory of some of the Defence witnesses. The decision affects, the Trial Chamber, has noted about three witnesses. This is Vaso Antic, Dodek Tubakovic, and Stefan Nikolic. So the Trial Chamber wanted to find out from the Prosecution what they would like to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution would be content to tender the parts of the 92 bis witnesses which we say are inconsistent with the witness's evidence in respect of Nikolic, and Mr. Tubakovic. The difficulty, of course, with Mr. Antic, Vaso Antic, is the appeal was on the basis of his not being allowed to refresh his memory from a statement, and merely tendering the statement would not allow him to refresh his memory as the Appeals Chamber says he should be allowed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I did discuss this briefly with my colleagues from the Defence. I understand Defence of Mr. Zaric would want the two witnesses recalled to explain why there are differing versions. And I understand Mr. Tadic's Defence is content with our tendering of those portions. The Prosecution is basically in the Trial Chamber's hands on this. We don't wish to unnecessarily prolong things or bring people back because our submission will be our witnesses have said one thing, and their witnesses have said two different things; therefore, our witness is more reliable. But if the Trial Chamber wishes to hear from the witness and hear the explanation, we, of course, wouldn't oppose that. But as I say, in the case of Mr. Antic, I can't really see a practical solution other than his recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I should state the position of Mr. Zaric Defence. This is not what was our position regarding those two. I still haven't had the opportunity to discuss this issue with Mr. Zaric because we have received this decision of the Appeals Chamber right before these proceedings started in the afternoon, and this was not the position of ours. Furthermore, I think that we will not ask for these two witnesses to be brought back to The Hague and to give their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Before I go to Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lazarevic, so you have stated your position in spite of the fact that you haven't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did. We don't ask these two witnesses to come again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Tadic's Defence, we shall neither insist on recalling Mr. Tubakovic for, I would say, a very simple reason. I'd like him to come back and clear these matters up, but when Mr. Tubakovic finished his testimony, he was relieved of any further testimony. I talked with him. It was just an ordinary conversation, and we talked about it. What I mean to say is that if a witness is recalled to testify about his testimony, with all due respect to the Appeals Chamber, if the witness was released and if the Prosecutor asks him, "did you discuss this subject with the Defence counsel," then obviously the validity of the words of his testimony will be less. So in my closing argument, I will also express my argument how is one to weigh, to judge, what their witness has not testified about. But I do not object to tendering that part of the statement into evidence for the appreciation by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is, you are speaking for the witness -- regarding the Witness Tubakovic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you are speaking in connection with Vaso Antic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on behalf of my client for witnesses Nikolic and Vaso Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What about the Prosecution's proposal that they would tender that part of the evidence which is being disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So that leaves us with Vaso Antic and the point which the Prosecution pointed out, that...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it goes further. The difference is the intended purpose with Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Tubakovic was impeachment. With Mr. Antic, his statement actually goes to the acts and conduct of the accused, that is, that Mr. Simic -- Dr. Simic telephoned him. So that can't be admitted for the purpose of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, it can't. This is what I'm saying. Because the other two, that could be dealt with admitting the parts that were disputed. But with Vaso Antic, it seems appears he has to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But that appears to be the difficulty with that approach, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In that case, then the Trial Chamber has decided that Mr. Vaso Antic will have to come back to complete the evidence. The Victims and Witnesses Unit will be informed so that they can locate him and try to bring him at the earliest opportunity possible, and the parties will be told as to the date and time. I think we've come to the end of our proceedings. We show our appreciation to the supporting staff. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: at 7.23 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned sine die
